AltText: The fissured, nearly vertical northern face of Beinn Tharsuinn Chaol viewed from A’ Mhaighdean in the Fisherfield Forest in early morning light.
Title: Beinn Tharsuinn Chaol from A’ Mhaighdean
Description:
Beinn Tharsuinn Chaol presents its dramatic, fissured northern face to A’ Mhaighdean, generally reckoned to be the most remote Munro. There’s quite a striking difference between the names of these two mountains. One translates to the poetic and intriguing ”The Maiden”, the other to the much more prosaic “narrow transverse mountain”.

I’ve always had this vague idea that I will compleat the Munros one day (yes that’s how you spell it, in case you didn’t know), but I’ve never been in much of a rush about it. One occasion that illustrates this lack of urgency is when I came within less than 100m of the top of Cairn Gorm, but passed up the rather tempting opportunity to tick one off the list in order to allow myself more time to take a detour along the River Avon on my way to camp at Loch Etchachan. Similarly, a more dedicated Munroist than me might, if they had spent a whole week in a cottage at the foot of Mull’s one and only Munro (and furthermore only twenty metres from the only path to the top), have had a saunter up there at some point.

It hasn’t escaped my notice that the maths doesn’t quite stack up. To date, since my first trip to Scotland in 2017, I have only summited 9 Munros despite making at least one trip to Scotland every year since. That’s a paltry rate of one per year. So unless they make significant strides in medical science I really will need to get a move on if I’m going to have any chance of becoming a compleatist. That said, I think there’s much to be said for going slow. Imagine not having any new Munros to climb. Quinn Young, a Scottish girl who conquered all of the Munros aged just ten said “I feel proud of myself, but also a little upset because the adventure with my dad’s kind of finished.”.

I took this photo during a circuit of the Fisherfield 6, the morning after camping on A’ Mhaighdean. That was my most fruitful trip so far, as far as Munro bagging goes, with five Munros over the course of two days.
